stem: Why is the entropy $H(X)=-\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)$ a sensible measure of the information in a source?
correct: It is the average surprise $-\log p(X)$ of an outcome, so rarer outcomes carry more information.
It is the expected surprise of one outcome, with rare outcomes the most surprising.

distractors.text: It is the number of different outcomes the source can produce, whatever their probabilities.
distractors.misconception: confuses entropy with the alphabet size

distractors.text: It is the probability of the most likely outcome, since likely outcomes carry the information.
distractors.misconception: reverses the role of rare and common outcomes

distractors.text: It is the variance of the outcomes, which measures how spread out they are.
It is the average of the outcome probabilities, weighted by the outcome values.
distractors.misconception: confuses entropy with an expectation of the values

distractors.text: It is the length of the shortest description of the most likely outcome only.
distractors.misconception: ignores the averaging over all outcomes

explanation: The self-information $-\log p(x)$ is large for rare outcomes; entropy averages it. It depends only on the probabilities, not on the labels or numerical values of the outcomes.

stem: A source takes $M$ values. For which distribution is $H(X)$ largest, and what is that largest value?
correct: The uniform distribution, with maximum entropy $\log M$ bits for a base-2 logarithm.
Equally likely values, giving entropy $\log_2 M$.

distractors.text: A distribution with one value of probability close to 1, giving entropy close to $\log M$.
distractors.misconception: believes a concentrated distribution is the most uncertain

distractors.text: Any distribution on $M$ values, since all of them have entropy exactly equal to $\log M$.
distractors.misconception: thinks entropy depends only on the alphabet size

distractors.text: The geometric-like distribution $p_i\propto 2^{-i}$, with entropy about $M$ bits.
distractors.misconception: confuses a dyadic distribution with the maximiser

distractors.text: The uniform distribution, with maximum entropy $M$ bits for any alphabet size.
distractors.misconception: forgets the logarithm in the maximum

distractors.text: A two-point distribution on the extreme values, with entropy $\log 2$ bits.
distractors.misconception: confuses spread of the values with entropy

explanation: By Jensen (or $D(p\|u)\ge 0$), $H(X)\le\log M$ with equality iff $p$ is uniform. A nearly deterministic source has entropy near 0.

stem: Let $Y=g(X)$ for a deterministic function $g$. Which statement about entropies holds?
correct: $H(Y)\le H(X)$, with equality when $g$ is one-to-one on the values taken by $X$.
A deterministic function of a variable cannot raise its entropy.

distractors.text: $H(Y)\ge H(X)$, because applying a function can only add information.
$H(Y)=H(X)$ for every function $g$, since $Y$ is determined by $X$.
distractors.misconception: confuses determination of Y by X with the reverse

distractors.text: $H(Y)$ and $H(X)$ are unrelated, since the function may map to any alphabet.
distractors.misconception: ignores the many-to-one collapse of probabilities

distractors.text: $H(Y)\le H(X)$ with equality only when $g$ is constant.
$H(Y)=0$, because $Y$ is a deterministic function of $X$.
distractors.misconception: confuses a function of X with a constant

explanation: Merging outcomes can only lose information: $H(X)=H(X,g(X))=H(g(X))+H(X|g(X))\ge H(g(X))$.

stem: Why does the choice of the base of the logarithm in the entropy matter little?
correct: Changing the base multiplies $H(X)$ by a constant factor, so only the unit changes.
Entropies in two bases differ by a fixed multiplicative constant.

distractors.text: Different bases give a different ordering of sources by entropy, so the base must be agreed in advance.
distractors.misconception: thinks the base changes comparisons between sources

distractors.text: Entropy is only defined for base 2, so other bases must be converted by a table.
distractors.misconception: thinks bits are the only possible unit

distractors.text: Changing the base adds a constant to $H(X)$, as with a change of origin.
distractors.misconception: confuses a scale factor with a shift

distractors.text: Changing the base changes the probabilities but not the values of the outcomes.
distractors.misconception: confuses the base with the distribution

distractors.text: The base only matters when the alphabet is infinite.
distractors.misconception: restricts the unit change to a special case

explanation: $\log_b x=\log_a x/\log_a b$, so $H_b(X)=H_a(X)/\log_a b$. The unit is bits for base 2 and nats for base $e$.

stem: Two independent events have probabilities $p$ and $q$. How do their self-informations $-\log p$ and $-\log q$ combine for the joint event?
correct: They add: the joint event has self-information $-\log p-\log q$.
The information of the two events is the sum of the two.

distractors.text: They multiply, since the probabilities multiply.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the logarithm turns products into sums

distractors.text: The joint event has the larger of the two informations.
They average, since information is an expectation.
They subtract, since independent events cancel each other.
The joint event has the smaller of the two informations.

explanation: $-\log(pq)=-\log p-\log q$. Additivity over independent events is the property that singles out the logarithm.

stem: Which identity is the chain rule for entropy?
correct: $H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y|X)$, whether or not $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
Joint entropy is the entropy of $X$ plus what $Y$ adds.

distractors.text: $H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y)$ for all $X$ and $Y$, whether or not they are dependent.
$H(X,Y)=H(X|Y)+H(Y|X)$, since each variable is explained by the other.
$H(X,Y)=H(X)-H(Y|X)$, since conditioning removes information.
$H(X,Y)=\max\{H(X),H(Y)\}$, since the larger variable determines the other.
distractors.misconception: confuses the joint with the larger marginal

explanation: By $p(x,y)=p(x)p(y|x)$ and taking $-E\log$. In general $H(X,Y)\le H(X)+H(Y)$, with equality iff $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

stem: Which statement about conditioning and entropy is correct?
correct: $H(X|Y)\le H(X)$ on average, though a single value $y$ may raise it.
Conditioning never raises the average entropy.

distractors.text: $H(X|Y=y)\le H(X)$ for every single value $y$ of $Y$.
distractors.misconception: applies the average statement to each outcome

distractors.text: $H(X|Y)\ge H(X)$, since extra variables make the problem more complicated.
$H(X|Y)=H(X)$ unless $Y$ is a function of $X$.
$H(X|Y)\le H(X)$ with equality iff $X$ is a function of $Y$.
$H(X|Y)<H(X)$ strictly, whatever the joint distribution.

explanation: $H(X)-H(X|Y)=I(X;Y)\ge 0$, with equality iff independent. A single observation $y$ can be misleading and raise the uncertainty, but not on average.

stem: What are the basic properties of the Kullback-Leibler divergence $D(p\|q)$ between two distributions?
correct: $D(p\|q)\ge0$ with equality iff $p=q$, but in general $D(p\|q)\ne D(q\|p)$.
Never negative, zero only if $p=q$, and asymmetric.

distractors.text: $D(p\|q)=D(q\|p)$ always, so it is a genuine distance between distributions.
distractors.misconception: treats KL divergence as a symmetric metric

distractors.text: $D(p\|q)$ can be negative when $q$ puts more mass than $p$ on some outcomes.
$D(p\|q)$ is finite for any pair $p,q$ on the same alphabet.
distractors.misconception: ignores infinity when q vanishes where p does not

distractors.text: It satisfies the triangle inequality, $D(p\|r)\le D(p\|q)+D(q\|r)$.
$D(p\|q)=0$ whenever $p$ and $q$ have the same entropy.
distractors.misconception: confuses equal entropies with equal distributions

explanation: Gibbs' inequality follows from Jensen. KL divergence is not symmetric, fails the triangle inequality, and is infinite if $p(x)>0=q(x)$ for some $x$.

stem: How is the mutual information $I(X;Y)$ characterised?
correct: It equals $D(p(x,y)\|p(x)p(y))$, and is zero iff $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
$H(X)-H(X|Y)$, the uncertainty about $X$ that $Y$ removes.

distractors.text: It is zero iff $X$ and $Y$ are uncorrelated, since correlation measures dependence.
It is the sum $H(X)+H(Y)$, the total information in the two variables.
distractors.misconception: forgets the joint entropy in the definition

distractors.text: It can be negative when $X$ and $Y$ are negatively dependent.
distractors.misconception: confuses it with the sign of correlation

distractors.text: It is the conditional entropy $H(X|Y)$, the uncertainty that remains.
distractors.misconception: confuses the removed with the remaining uncertainty

distractors.text: It satisfies $I(X;Y)\le H(X)$ with equality iff $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

explanation: $I(X;Y)\ge 0$ with equality iff independent. Uncorrelated variables can have positive mutual information, for example $Y=X^2$ with $X$ symmetric.

stem: $X\to Y\to Z$ is a Markov chain. Which statement is the data-processing inequality?
correct: $I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y)$: processing cannot add information about $X$.
Processing cannot create information.

distractors.text: $I(X;Z)\ge I(X;Y)$, since $Z$ is computed from more data.
$I(X;Z)=I(X;Y)$ for every Markov chain.
distractors.misconception: thinks the chain structure preserves information

distractors.text: $I(X;Z)=I(X;Y)+I(Y;Z)$, as information adds along the chain.
distractors.misconception: treats mutual information as additive along a chain

distractors.text: $H(X|Z)\le H(X|Y)$, so $Z$ is at least as informative about $X$ as $Y$.
$I(X;Z)\le I(X;Y)$ needs $Z$ to be a one-to-one function of $Y$.
distractors.misconception: restricts the inequality to invertible maps

explanation: By the chain rule $I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Y)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z)\ge I(X;Z)$, since $I(X;Z|Y)=0$ for a Markov chain. It holds for any processing, including noisy.

stem: In the information diagram of two variables $X$ and $Y$, which region corresponds to $I(X;Y)$?
correct: The intersection of the sets $\tilde X$ and $\tilde Y$, while $H(X,Y)$ is their union.
The overlap of the two sets $\tilde X$ and $\tilde Y$ in the diagram.

distractors.text: The set difference $\tilde X\setminus\tilde Y$, the part of $X$ not explained by $Y$.
distractors.misconception: confuses mutual information with conditional entropy

distractors.text: The symmetric difference $\tilde X\triangle\tilde Y$, where exactly one of the variables is present.
distractors.misconception: confuses the overlap with the non-overlap

distractors.text: The union $\tilde X\cup\tilde Y$, the total information in the two variables.
The whole sample space, whose measure is always 1.
distractors.misconception: confuses the information measure with a probability measure

distractors.text: The complement of $\tilde X\cup\tilde Y$, the information in neither variable.
distractors.misconception: confuses the empty region with the overlap

explanation: With $\mu^*(\tilde X)=H(X)$, $\mu^*(\tilde X\cap\tilde Y)=I(X;Y)$, $\mu^*(\tilde X\setminus\tilde Y)=H(X|Y)$ and $\mu^*(\tilde X\cup\tilde Y)=H(X,Y)$.

stem: For three variables, which statement about the I-measure $\mu^*$ is true?
correct: The atom $\tilde X\cap\tilde Y\cap\tilde Z$ can have negative measure, so $\mu^*$ is not a measure in the usual sense.
$I(X;Y;Z)$ can be negative, for example when $Z=X\oplus Y$ for fair independent bits.

distractors.text: Every atom has non-negative measure, as the measure of a set cannot be negative.
distractors.misconception: assumes information diagrams behave like probability areas

distractors.text: The measure of every atom is non-negative, because every Shannon measure is non-negative.
distractors.misconception: extends the non-negativity of I(X;Y|Z) to all atoms

distractors.text: The three-way term is negative only when the variables are dependent in pairs.
distractors.misconception: misidentifies the example of three-way dependence

distractors.text: The three-way term is always zero, since three variables cannot overlap in information.
The triple intersection is non-negative whenever two of the variables are independent.

explanation: With $X,Y$ independent fair bits and $Z=X\oplus Y$: $I(X;Y)=0$ but $I(X;Y|Z)=1$, so $\mu^*(\tilde X\cap\tilde Y\cap\tilde Z)=I(X;Y)-I(X;Y|Z)=-1$.

stem: Which identity can be read directly from the information diagram of $X$ and $Y$?
correct: $H(X)=H(X|Y)+I(X;Y)$, which can be read directly off the diagram of two variables.
$\tilde X$ is the union of $\tilde X\setminus\tilde Y$ and $\tilde X\cap\tilde Y$, two disjoint parts.

distractors.text: $H(X|Y)=H(X)+I(X;Y)$, since conditioning adds the overlap.
distractors.misconception: gets the sign of the overlap wrong

distractors.text: $I(X;Y)=H(X)H(Y)$, the overlap of two sets of measures $H(X)$ and $H(Y)$.

explanation: The region $\tilde X$ is the disjoint union of $\tilde X\setminus\tilde Y$ and $\tilde X\cap\tilde Y$. The joint entropy is $H(X)+H(Y)-I(X;Y)$.

stem: $X\to Y\to Z$ is a Markov chain. What does this say in the information diagram?
correct: The atom $\tilde X\cap\tilde Z\setminus\tilde Y$ has zero measure, that is, $I(X;Z|Y)=0$.
Given $Y$, no information is shared between $X$ and $Z$.

distractors.text: The atom $\tilde X\cap\tilde Y\cap\tilde Z$ has measure zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses the triple overlap with the conditional overlap

distractors.text: The sets $\tilde X$ and $\tilde Z$ are disjoint, so $I(X;Z)=0$.
The sets $\tilde X$ and $\tilde Y$ are disjoint, so $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the chain starts with a dependence

distractors.text: The atom $\tilde X\cap\tilde Y\setminus\tilde Z$ has measure zero, so $I(X;Y|Z)=0$.
distractors.misconception: confuses with a different conditional independence

distractors.text: The atom $\tilde Y\setminus(\tilde X\cup\tilde Z)$ has measure zero, so $H(Y|X,Z)=0$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the Markov property with determinism

explanation: The Markov property is $I(X;Z|Y)=0$, the measure of the atom in $\tilde X\cap\tilde Z$ but outside $\tilde Y$. The triple overlap can still be non-zero.

stem: How many atoms does the information diagram of $n$ random variables have?
correct: There are $2^n-1$ atoms, one per non-empty subset.
Counting the non-empty subsets of the variables gives it.

distractors.text: There are $2^n$ atoms, one of them being the region outside every set.
distractors.misconception: counts the empty region as an atom

distractors.text: There are $n$ atoms, one per variable.
There are $n(n-1)/2$ atoms, one for each pair of variables.
There are $2^{n-1}$ atoms, one for each subset of even size.
There are $n!$ atoms, one for each ordering of the variables.

explanation: Atoms are indexed by non-empty subsets $G$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, those inside the sets of $G$ and outside the others; the region outside every set is excluded because its measure is 0.

stem: What does the Kraft inequality say about a binary prefix code with codeword lengths $l_1,\dots,l_m$?
correct: $\sum_i2^{-l_i}\le1$, and any such lengths allow a prefix code.
A prefix code exists iff $\sum_i2^{-l_i}\le1$ for these lengths.

distractors.text: $\sum_i l_i\le 1$, so that the codeword lengths are summable.
$\sum_i 2^{-l_i}=1$ for every prefix code, with equality exactly.
$\sum_i 2^{-l_i}\ge 1$, since the code must cover all binary strings.
$\sum_i 2^{-l_i}\le 1$ is needed for a prefix code, but then a code with those lengths might still fail to exist.
$\sum_i l_i 2^{-l_i}\le 1$, so that the expected length is at most one.

explanation: Each codeword of length $l$ in a prefix code occupies a fraction $2^{-l}$ of the code tree's leaves, and the subtrees are disjoint; the converse builds the code level by level.

stem: Which statement about the Huffman code for a given distribution is correct?
correct: Merging the two least likely symbols repeatedly builds a minimal prefix code.
Among all prefix codes, Huffman codes have the smallest average length.

distractors.text: It minimises the length of the longest codeword, rather than the expected length.
distractors.misconception: confuses average length with worst-case length

distractors.text: It assigns the shortest codeword to the least probable symbol.
It is the unique optimal code, so any other optimal code is a relabelling of it.
distractors.misconception: forgets ties and different tree shapes

distractors.text: Merging the two most probable symbols first gives the minimal expected length.
It has expected length exactly equal to $H(X)$ for every source.

explanation: The two least likely symbols can be taken as siblings at the deepest level in some optimal code, which reduces the problem to $m-1$ symbols; induction gives optimality.

stem: A source with entropy $H(X)$ is encoded by an optimal binary prefix code with expected length $L$. Which relation holds?
correct: $H(X)\le L<H(X)+1$, so the average length is within one bit of the entropy.
Entropy bounds $L$ from below, and $L$ stays within one bit of it.

distractors.text: $L\le H(X)$, since the code compresses the source.
$L=H(X)$ for every source, since the code is optimal.
distractors.misconception: thinks optimal codes always meet the entropy

distractors.text: $L\ge H(X)+1$, since an integer number of bits is needed per symbol.
distractors.misconception: turns the upper bound into a lower bound

distractors.text: $H(X)-1<L\le H(X)$, since rounding lengths down gives a code.
distractors.misconception: confuses rounding up with rounding down

distractors.text: $L<H(X)$ for sources with many symbols, because the code uses fewer bits than the entropy.
distractors.misconception: thinks large alphabets beat the entropy

explanation: Lengths $l_i=\lceil-\log p_i\rceil$ satisfy Kraft and give $L<H+1$; the lower bound $L\ge H$ is Gibbs' inequality combined with the Kraft sum being at most 1. Equality $L=H$ holds iff all $p_i$ are powers of $1/2$.

stem: When is the expected length of an optimal binary prefix code exactly equal to the entropy?
correct: When each probability is a power of $1/2$, that is, dyadic.
For dyadic distributions only.

distractors.text: When the source has only two symbols.
distractors.misconception: forgets that a binary source can have entropy below one bit

distractors.text: When all symbol probabilities are different.
When the number of symbols is a power of 2.
When the distribution is uniform on any number of symbols.
distractors.misconception: misses that uniform needs a power-of-two size

distractors.text: Never, because the expected length always exceeds the entropy strictly.

explanation: $L-H(X)=\sum_i p_i\log\{p_i/2^{-l_i}\}$ vanishes iff $p_i=2^{-l_i}$ for all $i$. A binary source with $p=(0.9,0.1)$ has $H<1$ but $L=1$.

stem: Which statement about Huffman codes for the same source is true?
correct: Different Huffman codes may exist for the source, all having the same expected length.
Ties in the merging steps can change codeword lengths without changing the average.

distractors.text: The Huffman code is unique up to relabelling the 0 and 1 branches.
Different Huffman codes can have different expected lengths, one of them being better.
distractors.misconception: forgets that all choices remain optimal

distractors.text: Every Huffman code gives each symbol the same length as every other Huffman code.
distractors.misconception: confuses the average length with the individual lengths

distractors.text: A Huffman code is uniquely decodable only if the probabilities are all different.
Huffman codes are optimal only among codes with the same maximum length.

explanation: Ties can be resolved differently, giving different length profiles (for instance, probabilities $0.4,0.2,0.2,0.1,0.1$) but the same optimal average; the variance of the lengths may differ.

stem: What is the content of the weak asymptotic equipartition property for an i.i.d. source $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with entropy $H$?
correct: $-\frac1n\log p(X_1,\dots,X_n)\to H$ in probability, for an i.i.d. source.
Log-probability per symbol concentrates at $H$.

distractors.text: Every sequence of length $n$ has probability close to $2^{-nH}$.
distractors.misconception: applies the concentration to all sequences

distractors.text: $-\frac1n\log p(X_1,\dots,X_n)\to\log|\mathcal X|$, the log of the alphabet size.
distractors.misconception: confuses entropy with the maximum entropy

distractors.text: The sample mean of the symbols converges to $H$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the log-probability average with the symbol average

distractors.text: The number of sequences with positive probability is close to $2^{nH}$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the support with the typical set

distractors.text: The sequence probability $p(X^n)$ converges to a constant.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the probability decays exponentially

explanation: Apply the weak law of large numbers to the i.i.d. variables $-\log p(X_i)$ whose mean is $H$. Only most of the probability, not every sequence, lies near $2^{-nH}$.

stem: What can be said about the weakly typical set $A_\epsilon^{(n)}$ for large $n$?
correct: It has probability near 1 and about $2^{nH}$ members, each of probability about $2^{-nH}$.
Roughly $2^{nH}$ nearly equiprobable sequences carry almost all the mass.

distractors.text: It contains almost all sequences of length $n$, about $|\mathcal X|^n$ of them.
distractors.misconception: confuses the typical set with the full space

distractors.text: It contains the sequences with the largest probabilities and has size close to 1.
distractors.misconception: confuses typical with the single most probable sequence

distractors.text: It has probability close to 0, but contains a majority of the sequences.
distractors.misconception: reverses the probability and counting statements

distractors.text: It has about $2^{nH}$ elements, whose probabilities differ widely from each other.
It has about $nH$ elements, one for each unit of entropy.

explanation: The size is at most $2^{n(H+\epsilon)}$ because each member has probability at least $2^{-n(H+\epsilon)}$, and for large $n$ it is at least $(1-\epsilon)2^{n(H-\epsilon)}$.

stem: What does the source coding theorem for i.i.d. sources say about the compression rate $R$ in bits per symbol?
correct: Rates $R>H$ allow reliable block compression, and rates $R<H$ do not allow it.
Entropy is the threshold for the reliable compression of long blocks.

distractors.text: Any rate $R>0$ allows error-free compression when the block length is long enough.
Only rates $R\ge\log_2|\mathcal X|$ allow reliable compression.
distractors.misconception: confuses entropy with the alphabet size

distractors.text: Rates $R<H$ are possible provided the code is allowed a small probability of error that does not vanish.
distractors.misconception: confuses a fixed error with vanishing error

distractors.text: Rates $R>H$ are impossible, since $H$ is the minimum number of bits per symbol.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction of the threshold

distractors.text: Zero-error compression at rate $R=H$ is always possible with fixed-length blocks.
distractors.misconception: confuses vanishing error with zero error

explanation: Index the typical set with $n(H+\epsilon)$ bits and code everything else arbitrarily; the converse follows since $2^{nR}$ sequences cannot carry probability close to 1 if $R<H$.

stem: A binary source has $P(1)=0.1$. Is the single most probable sequence of length $n$, the all-zero sequence, in the typical set for large $n$?
correct: No: its log-probability per symbol is $-\log0.9$, which is not near $H$, so it is not typical.
It is more probable than any typical sequence, but it is not typical itself.

distractors.text: Yes, since a typical set must contain the most probable sequence.
Yes, since the all-zero sequence has the highest probability and probabilities decay as $2^{-nH}$.
No, because its probability is smaller than $2^{-n(H+\epsilon)}$.
distractors.misconception: reverses which side of the typical range it lies on

distractors.text: Yes, because its empirical frequencies equal the true probability of the symbol 0.
distractors.misconception: confuses the sequence with a typical type

distractors.text: It is typical for every $n$, but its probability tends to zero.
distractors.misconception: mixes up typical status with vanishing probability

explanation: The all-zero sequence has probability $0.9^n$, larger than $2^{-nH}$ with $H=h(0.1)\approx0.47$ since $-\log_2 0.9\approx0.15<H$. Its total mass is tiny; typical sequences have about $0.1n$ ones.

stem: Why is weak typicality enough for the source coding theorem, even though weakly typical sequences need not have the right symbol frequencies?
correct: Only the sequence probability matters for counting: members have probability near $2^{-nH}$.
The counting argument needs the probabilities of sequences, not their symbol frequencies.

distractors.text: Because weakly typical sequences have exactly the right symbol frequencies for any source.
Because the theorem only holds for sources with uniform distributions.
Because the typical set is chosen to be independent of the source distribution.
distractors.misconception: ignores that typicality is defined through the source

distractors.text: Because compression needs only a rate larger than the log of the alphabet size.
distractors.misconception: confuses with the trivial fixed-length rate

distractors.text: Because the theorem is proved from the central limit theorem rather than the law of large numbers.

explanation: Weak typicality is defined by $|-\frac1n\log p(x^n)-H|\le\epsilon$ and is enough for the AEP; strong typicality (frequencies) is needed for finer results such as joint typicality arguments with channels.

stem: How is a strongly typical sequence defined for a finite-alphabet source with distribution $p$?
correct: Each symbol's relative frequency is within $\delta$ of its probability.
The empirical distribution is close to $p$ in every component.

distractors.text: Its probability is within $2^{\pm n\delta}$ of $2^{-nH}$.
Its first symbol has the highest probability and its last has the lowest.
Its empirical entropy equals the true entropy of the source exactly.
Its relative frequency of the most probable symbol is close to 1.
distractors.misconception: confuses frequencies with a concentration on one symbol

distractors.text: Its symbols are pairwise different.

explanation: Strong typicality bounds $|N(a;x^n)/n-p(a)|$ for every symbol $a$. It implies weak typicality (with a larger $\epsilon$), but not conversely.

stem: Which statement relates strong and weak typicality?
correct: A strongly typical sequence is weakly typical too (for a suitable $\epsilon$), but not conversely.
For a finite alphabet, strong typicality is the more demanding notion.

distractors.text: Weak and strong typicality define the same set of sequences.
Every weakly typical sequence is strongly typical, as the entropy fixes the frequencies.
Strong typicality is defined only for continuous variables.
Strong typicality is weaker, since it only fixes the most frequent symbol.
Strongly typical sequences exist only if the source is uniform.

explanation: Different frequency vectors can give the same value of $-\frac1n\log p(x^n)$, and weak typicality only controls that one number, not the individual frequencies.

stem: Why is strong typicality used in the proof of the channel coding theorem?
correct: It lets one count the output sequences jointly typical with a given input.
Jointly typical pairs have frequencies near $p(x,y)$.

distractors.text: It makes the channel noiseless on the typical set.
distractors.misconception: confuses typicality with absence of noise

distractors.text: It shows that every input sequence is jointly typical with every output sequence.
It ensures that the capacity equals the entropy of the source.
It replaces the need for random coding by a deterministic code construction.
It guarantees zero error for each message in the code.
distractors.misconception: confuses vanishing error with zero error

explanation: Strong typicality gives control over frequency counts of pairs $(x,y)$, and so over conditional typicality: the number of $y^n$ jointly typical with a typical $x^n$ is about $2^{nH(Y|X)}$.

stem: An independent input $\tilde X^n$ and output $Y^n$ are drawn from the marginals of a pair $(X,Y)$ with mutual information $I(X;Y)$. What is the probability that they are jointly typical?
correct: It is about $2^{-nI(X;Y)}$, which is small when $I(X;Y)>0$.
It is exponentially small, with exponent equal to $I(X;Y)$.

distractors.text: It is about $2^{-nH(X,Y)}$, the probability of one joint sequence.
distractors.misconception: confuses the pair set with a single pair

distractors.text: It is close to 1, because both are drawn from the right marginals.
It is about $2^{nI(X;Y)}$, which is large.
distractors.misconception: gets the sign of the exponent wrong

distractors.text: It is exactly $0$ for any $n$ when $I(X;Y)>0$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the probability is positive

distractors.text: It is about $2^{-nH(X)}$ regardless of the mutual information.
distractors.misconception: ignores the dependence of the pair

explanation: There are about $2^{nH(X,Y)}$ jointly typical pairs, each of probability about $2^{-n(H(X)+H(Y))}$ under independence, giving the total $2^{-n(H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y))}=2^{-nI(X;Y)}$.

stem: How many sequences have a given type (empirical distribution) $P$ with probabilities $P(a)$, as $n$ grows?
correct: About $2^{nH(P)}$ sequences have that type, where $H(P)$ is its entropy.
Exponentially many in $n$, at rate equal to the entropy of the type.

distractors.text: About $2^{nH(p)}$ with $p$ the true source distribution, whatever the type.
distractors.misconception: confuses the type with the source

distractors.text: Exactly $n!$ sequences, for any type.
About $|\mathcal X|^n$ sequences, because any arrangement is allowed.
About $nH(P)$ sequences.
Exactly one sequence, the sorted one.
distractors.misconception: confuses a type with a sequence

explanation: The type class has $n!/\prod_a (nP(a))!$ elements, between $(n+1)^{-|\mathcal X|}2^{nH(P)}$ and $2^{nH(P)}$ (Stirling). Strongly typical sequences belong to types near $p$.

stem: How is the capacity $C$ of a discrete memoryless channel $p(y|x)$ defined?
correct: $C=\max_{p(x)}I(X;Y)$, the maximum over inputs.
The maximum, over inputs, of the information in the output.

distractors.text: $C=\max_{p(x)} H(Y)$, the largest output entropy.
$C=\max_{p(x)} H(X)$, the largest input entropy.
$C=\min_{p(x)} I(X;Y)$, the worst case over inputs.
distractors.misconception: swaps the maximum for a minimum

distractors.text: $C=I(X;Y)$ for the uniform input, whatever the channel.
distractors.misconception: assumes the uniform input is always optimal

distractors.text: $C=\max_{p(x)} H(X|Y)$, the largest uncertainty after observation.

explanation: $I(X;Y)$ is a function of $p(x)$ for the fixed channel, concave in $p(x)$. The uniform input is optimal for symmetric channels but not in general.

stem: What does the channel coding theorem say for a discrete memoryless channel with capacity $C$?
correct: Every rate below $C$ is achievable with error tending to 0, and no rate above $C$ is.
Reliable communication is possible exactly at rates below $C$ bits per use.

distractors.text: Rates below $C$ are achievable only with a positive error probability that cannot vanish.
Rates above $C$ are achievable if the codewords are long enough.
Every rate is achievable if the channel is used with feedback.
distractors.misconception: thinks feedback raises capacity of a DMC

distractors.text: Only rates equal to $C$ exactly are achievable.
distractors.misconception: confuses the supremum with the only achievable rate

distractors.text: Achievable rates are those below $H(X)$ of the source.

explanation: Random coding with jointly typical decoding gives vanishing error for $R<C$; Fano's inequality gives the converse for $R>C$. The coding gain is paid in block length and delay.

stem: What is the capacity of the binary symmetric channel with crossover probability $p$?
correct: $C=1-h(p)$ bits, with $h$ the binary entropy.
One minus the noise entropy.

distractors.text: $C=1-p$ bits, as each bit is lost with probability $p$.
$C=h(p)$ bits, the entropy of the noise.
$C=1-h(p)$ for $p\le1/2$ and $C=0$ for $p>1/2$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that flipped outputs can be relabelled

distractors.text: $C=1+h(p)$ bits, since the noise adds randomness.
$C=\log_2(1/p)$ bits.

explanation: $I(X;Y)=H(Y)-h(p)\le1-h(p)$ with equality for uniform input. $C=0$ at $p=1/2$ and $C=1$ at $p=0$ or $p=1$, since a channel that always flips is perfectly informative.

stem: Which statement describes the binary erasure channel with erasure probability $\varepsilon$?
correct: Its capacity is $1-\varepsilon$, and a uniform input achieves it.
The best rate is the fraction of symbols that are not erased.

distractors.text: Its capacity is $1-h(\varepsilon)$, as for the binary symmetric channel.
Its capacity is $h(\varepsilon)$, the entropy of the erasure event.
Its capacity is $1-\varepsilon$, but only when the receiver knows the input.
Its capacity is $(1-\varepsilon)^2$ since both input values can be erased.
Its capacity is $0$ for any $\varepsilon>0$, since information is lost.

explanation: $I(X;Y)=H(X)-H(X|Y)=(1-\varepsilon)H(X)$, maximised at $H(X)=1$ by the uniform input. Erased symbols are known to be missing, so no flips are mixed in.

stem: Which of the following is a property of the mutual information $I(X;Y)$ for a fixed channel?
correct: It is a concave function of the input distribution $p(x)$ for a fixed channel.
Mixing two input distributions does at least as well as averaging their values.

distractors.text: It is a convex function of the input distribution, so the maximum is at an extreme point.
It is a linear function of $p(x)$, so any input is as good as another.
It is a concave function of the channel $p(y|x)$ for a fixed input.
distractors.misconception: swaps the roles of input and channel

distractors.text: It is increasing in each probability $p(x)$.
It is concave in $p(x)$ only when the channel is symmetric.
distractors.misconception: restricts the concavity to a special case

explanation: For a fixed channel, $I(X;Y)$ is concave in $p(x)$ and (for a fixed input) convex in the channel; concavity makes the capacity optimisation a convex program.

stem: How is the rate-distortion function $R(D)$ of a source with distortion measure $d$ defined?
correct: $R(D)=\min I(X;\hat X)$ over conditional distributions with $E\,d(X,\hat X)\le D$.
Least mutual information between source and reproduction at distortion $D$.

distractors.text: $R(D)=\max I(X;\hat X)$ over conditional distributions with $E\,d(X,\hat X)\le D$.
$R(D)=H(X)-D$, a straight line in the allowed distortion.
distractors.misconception: replaces the optimisation by a formula

distractors.text: $R(D)=\min H(\hat X)$ over reproduction distributions with distortion at most $D$.
distractors.misconception: confuses mutual information with output entropy

distractors.text: $R(D)=\min I(X;\hat X)$ over conditional distributions with $d(x,\hat x)\le D$ for every pair.
distractors.misconception: requires the distortion for every pair, not on average

distractors.text: $R(D)=E\,d(X,\hat X)$ for the best code.

explanation: Minimising the information that the reproduction carries about the source, subject to the average-distortion constraint, gives the least rate; the minimum is over test channels.

stem: Which properties does the rate-distortion function $R(D)$ have?
correct: Non-increasing, convex, zero for large $D$.
Convex, falling to zero.

distractors.text: It is concave and increasing in $D$.
distractors.misconception: reverses the direction and the curvature

distractors.text: It is non-increasing and concave in $D$.
It is constant in $D$ for all $D\ge0$.
It is convex but may increase for large $D$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that larger tolerance cannot cost more

distractors.text: It reaches 0 only when $D=0$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the lossless end with the lossy end

explanation: Convexity follows from convexity of $I$ in the test channel and time-sharing between two test channels; $R(D)=0$ at $D_{\max}=\min_{\hat x}E\,d(X,\hat x)$ with a constant reproduction.

stem: What are the values of $R(D)$ at the two ends of the distortion range for a discrete source with Hamming distortion?
correct: $R(0)=H(X)$, and $R(D)=0$ once $D\ge D_{\max}$.
$H(X)$ at $D=0$, zero at large $D$.

distractors.text: $R(0)=0$ and $R(D)$ is largest for the largest $D$.
$R(0)=\log|\mathcal X|$ for any source distribution.
$R(D)=0$ only when $D=1$.
distractors.misconception: takes the largest possible distortion rather than the zero-rate point

distractors.text: $R(0)=H(X)$ and $R(D)>0$ for every $D<1$.
distractors.misconception: misses the zero-rate point for a skewed source

distractors.text: $R(0)=1$ bit for every binary source.

explanation: At $D=0$ the reproduction must equal $X$, so $R=I(X;X)=H(X)$. Guessing the most likely symbol always has distortion $1-\max_x p(x)$ with no information transmitted.

stem: What does the rate-distortion theorem state about lossy compression of an i.i.d. source at average distortion $D$?
correct: Rates above $R(D)$ are achievable at distortion near $D$; rates below are not.
$R(D)$ is the least number of bits per symbol at distortion $D$.

distractors.text: Rates above $R(D)$ are achievable only with distortion exactly zero.
Rates below $R(D)$ are achievable if the block length is long enough.
distractors.misconception: thinks long blocks beat the bound

distractors.text: The rate $R(D)$ can be achieved with single-symbol codes, without long blocks.
Rates above $H(X)$ are needed for any non-zero distortion.
$R(D)$ is the minimum rate for the worst-case distortion of each sequence.

explanation: Achievability uses a random codebook with jointly typical encoding; the converse uses $nR\ge I(X^n;\hat X^n)\ge\sum I(X_i;\hat X_i)\ge nR(E\,d)$ and convexity.

stem: For a Bernoulli($p$) source with $p\le1/2$ and Hamming distortion, what is $R(D)$ for $0\le D<p$?
correct: $h(p)-h(D)$ bits.

distractors.misconception: replaces the binary entropy of D by D

distractors.text: $R(D)=1-h(D)$, as for the binary symmetric channel.

distractors.misconception: applies the entropy to the difference

explanation: The test channel is a binary symmetric channel from $\hat X$ to $X$ with crossover $D$: $I(X;\hat X)=H(X)-H(X|\hat X)=h(p)-h(D)$. For $D\ge p$ the rate is 0.

stem: What is the idea of the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm for channel capacity?
correct: It alternately maximises over the input law and a backward channel.
Alternating maximisation in two steps.

distractors.text: It evaluates $I(X;Y)$ at the uniform input only.
distractors.misconception: confuses the algorithm with a single evaluation

distractors.text: It solves $\nabla I=0$ by Newton's method in the simplex.
It alternately maximises the input entropy and the output entropy.
It is a random search over input distributions.
It minimises $I(X;Y)$ by alternating between two minimisations.
distractors.misconception: swaps maximisation and minimisation for capacity

explanation: $C=\max_r\max_q\sum_x\sum_y r(x)W(y|x)\log\{q(x|y)/r(x)\}$; the best $q$ for a given $r$ is the posterior, and the best $r$ for a given $q$ is a normalised exponential.

stem: Which properties does Blahut-Arimoto have for capacity computation?
correct: The lower bound rises at every step and converges to $C$.
Monotone improvement, with limit $C$.

distractors.text: The bound can decrease for some steps and still converge.
It converges to a local maximum which may not be the capacity.
It needs the initial input distribution to be the optimal one.
distractors.misconception: confuses the start with the answer

distractors.text: It converges in a single step for any channel.
It converges to the capacity regardless of whether the start has zero entries.
distractors.misconception: forgets that zero entries stay at zero

explanation: Each step maximises a function of the pair $(r,q)$, so the objective never decreases; concavity of $I$ in $r$ means a stationary point is global. Zero entries of $r$ remain zero.

stem: In the Blahut-Arimoto capacity iteration, how is the new input distribution computed from the current one $r$?
correct: $r'(x)\propto r(x)\exp D(W(\cdot|x)\|q)$, with $q$ the output.
Reweight by the exponentiated divergence.

distractors.text: $r'(x)\propto r(x)D(W(\cdot|x)\|q)$, without the exponential.
$r'(x)\propto\exp(-D(W(\cdot|x)\|q))$, favouring rows close to the output.
$r'(x)=1/|\mathcal X|$ at every step.
distractors.misconception: confuses the update with uniform restart

distractors.text: $r'(x)\propto q(x)$, copying the output distribution.
$r'(x)\propto H(W(\cdot|x))$, favouring noisy rows.

explanation: Inputs whose rows are far (in divergence) from the current output distribution get more weight. At the optimum all used inputs have equal divergence, equal to $C$.

stem: Which stopping rule is available for the Blahut-Arimoto capacity algorithm?
correct: Stop when $\max_xD(W(\cdot|x)\|q)$ and the lower bound nearly agree.
Compare computable upper and lower bounds.

distractors.text: Stop after exactly $|\mathcal X|$ iterations, which is always enough.
Stop when the input distribution becomes uniform.
distractors.misconception: confuses the start with the end

distractors.text: Stop when the mutual information is positive.
Stop when the upper bound falls below the lower bound.
There is no stopping rule, because the iterates never converge.

explanation: $I(r)\le C\le\max_x D(W(\cdot|x)\|q)$ at each step, where $q$ is the output distribution of $r$; the gap tends to 0 as the iteration converges.

stem: What is the role of the slope parameter in the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm for the rate-distortion function?
correct: It picks the point of the $R(D)$ curve with that tangent slope.
One parameter value gives one point on the curve.

distractors.text: It is the number of iterations the algorithm is run for.
distractors.misconception: confuses the parameter with the iteration count

distractors.text: It is the block length of the source code.
It is the distortion level, which must be given as an input.
distractors.misconception: confuses the slope with the distortion

distractors.text: It is the probability of the least likely source symbol.
It is always set to zero to find the minimum rate.

explanation: The iteration minimises $I(X;\hat X)+s\,E\,d(X,\hat X)$ with $s<0$ the slope of $R(D)$; varying $s$ traces out the curve, and $D$ is an output of the iteration, not an input.

stem: Which statement about the differential entropy $h(X)=-\int f\log f$ of a continuous random variable is correct?
correct: It can be negative, for instance for $U(0,a)$ with $a<1$.
Unlike discrete entropy, it need not be non-negative.

distractors.text: It is always non-negative, as for discrete entropy.
It is always at most 0, since $f\le1$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the density with a probability

distractors.text: It equals the entropy of the discretised variable.
distractors.misconception: ignores the divergence as the grid is refined

distractors.text: It is the number of bits needed to describe $X$ exactly.
distractors.misconception: ignores that exact description needs infinite bits

distractors.text: It is non-negative if and only if $X$ has finite variance.

explanation: A density can exceed 1, so $-\log f$ can be negative. For $U(0,a)$, $h=\log a<0$ when $a<1$ (in bits).

stem: How does the differential entropy change under a linear transformation $Y=aX+b$ with $a\ne0$?
correct: $h(Y)=h(X)+\log|a|$, so a shift changes nothing but a scaling does.
Shifts do not matter.

distractors.text: $h(Y)=h(X)$, as for discrete entropy under a relabelling.
distractors.misconception: carries over invariance from the discrete case
treats entropy as a linear functional

distractors.text: $h(Y)=h(X)+b$, since only the shift matters.
distractors.misconception: confuses the shift with the scale

distractors.text: $h(Y)=h(X)-\log|a|$.
$h(Y)=h(X)+\log a^2$ for every real $a$.

explanation: $f_Y(y)=f_X((y-b)/a)/|a|$, so $-E\log f_Y(Y)=h(X)+\log|a|$. Mutual information, in contrast, is invariant under such invertible maps.

stem: Among all distributions on the real line with a given variance $\sigma^2$, which has the largest differential entropy?
correct: The normal distribution, with $h=\frac12\log(2\pi e\sigma^2)$.
The Gaussian maximises entropy for a fixed variance.

distractors.text: The uniform distribution with variance $\sigma^2$.
The exponential distribution with variance $\sigma^2$.
The Laplace distribution, since it has heavier tails.
None, because the supremum is infinite.
The distribution concentrated at two points.

explanation: By $D(f\|\phi)\ge0$ with $\phi$ the normal density of the same variance: $h(f)\le-\int f\log\phi=\frac12\log(2\pi e\sigma^2)$. The uniform on an interval has the maximum for bounded support, and the exponential for given mean on $[0,\infty)$.

stem: What is the relation between the discrete entropy of a finely quantised continuous variable and its differential entropy?
correct: $H(X^\Delta)\approx h(X)-\log\Delta$, unbounded as $\Delta\to0$.
It exceeds $h(X)$ by about $-\log\Delta$.

distractors.text: $H(X^\Delta)\to h(X)$ as $\Delta\to0$.
distractors.misconception: treats the differential entropy as a limit

distractors.text: $H(X^\Delta)\approx h(X)+\log\Delta$, which tends to $-\infty$.
distractors.misconception: gets the sign of the log wrong

distractors.text: $H(X^\Delta)$ does not depend on $\Delta$.
$H(X^\Delta)=h(X)$ exactly when $\Delta$ is a power of 2.
$H(X^\Delta)\le h(X)$, since quantisation loses information.

explanation: The probability of a bin is about $f(x)\Delta$, so $H=-\sum f\Delta\log(f\Delta)\approx h(X)-\log\Delta$. Differences such as mutual information do converge.

stem: Which quantities keep their discrete properties when passing to continuous variables?
correct: The divergence $D(f\|g)$ and the mutual information $I(X;Y)$ remain non-negative.
$D(f\|g)\ge0$ and $I(X;Y)\ge0$ still hold for densities.

distractors.text: The entropy $h(X)\ge0$ remains non-negative.
The mutual information can be negative, as the differential entropies can be.
distractors.misconception: confuses differences of h with I

distractors.text: The divergence $D(f\|g)$ is zero for any pair of densities with equal differential entropy.
distractors.misconception: confuses equal entropy with equal distribution

distractors.text: The divergence becomes symmetric.
The mutual information is infinite for any dependent continuous pair.

explanation: $I(X;Y)=h(X)-h(X|Y)=D(f_{XY}\|f_Xf_Y)\ge0$ by Jensen. Only the entropy itself loses non-negativity and invariance under invertible maps.

stem: Which maximum-entropy statement is correct?
correct: On $[0,\infty)$ with a given mean, the exponential maximises entropy.
For a fixed mean on the half-line, the exponential is optimal.

distractors.text: The normal distribution maximises it, since it has the largest entropy overall.
The uniform distribution on $[0,2\mu]$ maximises it for mean $\mu$.
The gamma distribution with shape 2 maximises it.
No density attains the maximum, because the supremum is infinite.
A point mass at the mean, as it has the smallest spread.
distractors.misconception: confuses the minimum with the maximum

explanation: With $f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, $D(g\|f)\ge0$ gives $h(g)\le1-\ln\lambda$ nats for all $g$ with mean $1/\lambda$; the bound is attained by $g=f$.

stem: What is the capacity of the discrete-time additive white Gaussian noise channel $Y=X+Z$, $Z\sim N(0,N)$, with average power constraint $E X^2\le P$?
correct: $C=\frac12\log(1+P/N)$ bits per channel use.
Half the logarithm of one plus the SNR.

distractors.text: $C=\frac12\log(P/N)$ bits per use.
$C=\log(1+P/N)$ bits per use.
distractors.misconception: forgets the one half for real signals

distractors.text: $C=P/N$ bits per use, linear in the signal-to-noise ratio.
$C=\frac12\log(1+P)$ bits per use, independent of the noise.
$C=\frac12\log(1+N/P)$ bits per use.

explanation: $I(X;Y)=h(Y)-h(Z)\le\frac12\log2\pi e(P+N)-\frac12\log2\pi eN$, with equality for Gaussian $X$. Capacity grows only logarithmically in the power.

stem: Why is the Gaussian input optimal for the additive Gaussian noise channel under a power constraint?
correct: $h(Y)$ is maximal for Gaussian $Y$, which a Gaussian input gives.
The output entropy is largest for a normal output.

distractors.text: Because a Gaussian input minimises the noise entropy $h(Z)$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the roles of input and noise

distractors.text: Because the Gaussian has the smallest entropy for a given variance.
Because the Gaussian input has no power constraint.
Because the Gaussian has the largest alphabet.
Because the Gaussian input makes the noise vanish.

explanation: $I=h(Y)-h(Z)$ with $h(Z)$ fixed; $\operatorname{Var}Y\le P+N$ and the normal maximises $h$ for given variance. A finite-alphabet input is suboptimal at high signal-to-noise ratios.

stem: What does the capacity formula imply when the power $P$ is increased with $N$ fixed?
correct: It grows without bound, but only logarithmically.
Slow, logarithmic growth.

distractors.text: Capacity grows linearly in $P$.
Capacity saturates at $\frac12\log(1+N)$.
Capacity is independent of $P$ once $P>N$.
Capacity grows like $\sqrt P$.
Capacity decreases for large $P$ because of interference.

explanation: At high SNR, $\frac12\log(1+P/N)\approx\frac12\log(P/N)$, so multiplying $P$ by 2 adds $\frac12$ bit per use. Bandwidth, not power, is the cheaper way to increase rate.

stem: For parallel Gaussian channels with noise variances $N_1,\dots,N_k$ and total power $P$, how is power allocated by water-filling?
correct: Set $P_i=(\nu-N_i)^+$ with $\sum P_i=P$, so noisier channels get less power.
Power fills up to a common level.

distractors.text: Allocate the same power $P/k$ to each channel, whatever its noise.
Allocate the most power to the noisiest channel to compensate for it.
Put all the power in the least noisy channel.
distractors.misconception: confuses the greedy with the optimal allocation

distractors.text: Allocate power proportional to the noise variance $N_i$.
Give each channel $P_i=\nu+N_i$ so that the totals are equal.
distractors.misconception: flips the sign of the noise

explanation: Maximise $\sum\frac12\log(1+P_i/N_i)$ subject to $\sum P_i=P$ and $P_i\ge0$ by KKT: $\frac{1}{2(N_i+P_i)}=\lambda$ on used channels, so $N_i+P_i=\nu$ is constant.

stem: What is the capacity of $k$ independent parallel Gaussian channels with a total power constraint?
correct: The sum $\sum_i\frac12\log(1+P_i/N_i)$ at the water-filling powers.
Each channel adds its own capacity.

distractors.text: The capacity of the best channel at the full power $P$.
distractors.misconception: ignores the use of other channels

distractors.text: The average of the individual capacities at equal power.
distractors.misconception: takes an average instead of a sum

distractors.text: $\frac12\log(1+P/\sum N_i)$, treating the noises as one.
The sum of capacities with every channel at power $P$.
The capacity of the worst channel, since it limits the rest.

explanation: Independent channels carry independent information, and the optimal input is independent Gaussian across channels, so the mutual information adds. Equal powers $P/k$ are suboptimal unless the noises are equal.
